text: Welcome. The central idea in this lecture is that stress is not just “more load” — it is pressure that reveals whether a system still behaves correctly. In a stateful concurrent system, the real question is whether the invariant survives when timing shifts, retries happen, queues build up, or multiple actors compete for the same resource. We will keep coming back to one professional habit: name the assumption, make the pressure visible, and collect evidence that proves what actually happened.

The key idea here is that stress is a design pressure, not just an accident. When a system is stressed, load, timing shifts, retries, queues, and contention start exposing whether the design really holds. A common mistake is to judge a system by one clean run. Instead, we ask a harder question: under pressure, does the invariant still hold? Good engineering makes that question measurable, observable, and testable.

This is where hidden assumptions become dangerous. A baseline design often assumes the workflow runs once, state changes happen in order, load never changes behavior, and failure evidence is optional. But reality is messier: concurrent runs overlap, timing affects what state is visible, pressure exposes limits, and evidence becomes necessary if you want to defend the design. So when a system looks correct on the happy path, we should ask what it is quietly assuming about execution.

Let's pause here and make the failure concrete. One sequential run can hide the real execution model, because the code may appear correct when nothing overlaps and nothing delays. Under pressure, the same workflow can interleave, delay, or even repeat. That means the failure is often not a syntax problem — it is a mismatch between the design assumption and the real execution environment. Repeatable pressure tests are how we expose that gap between intent and reality.

A common stress failure has a very recognizable shape. You start seeing latency spikes, duplicate work, missing completion logs, and queues that never seem to drain. The causes are usually uncomfortable but ordinary: slow dependencies, retry storms, stale state, or hidden coordination costs. What makes this serious is that the baseline version can look healthy until the system is pushed far enough to reveal the problem. That is exactly why we collect evidence under pressure, not just success screenshots.

This matters because stress claims are only defensible if they come with structured evidence. Useful evidence includes logs, traces, interleavings, and repeatable test output. Ideally, you want to show baseline behavior, failure behavior, and then the corrected behavior with its trade-off. Without that, a reviewer has to take your word for it, and that is not enough in an engineering defense. The point is to make the failure reproducible and the conclusion checkable.

When pressure reveals a weakness, the response should protect the invariant directly. You might use state guards or version checks to stop invalid transitions, backpressure or circuit breakers to limit damage, idempotency or deduplication to make duplicates safe, or compensation and reconciliation to recover after partial failure. The key idea is to choose the smallest control that preserves the relevant property. Every fix has a cost, so we do not pretend the solution is free.

Here the contrast is between hoping the happy path represents reality and deliberately engineering for pressure. Before the repair, teams often treat logs as optional and assume timing will cooperate. After the repair, they name the invariant, add structured evidence, and apply controls like backpressure, guards, or idempotency. That shift matters because a system is only mature when it can explain not just what worked, but what failed and how it recovered.

Let’s organize the vocabulary. Stress is pressure that exposes limits, contention is multiple actors fighting over the same resource, saturation is the point where more work makes performance worse, and edge cases are the rare timing combinations that appear only under load. In each case, the professional task is the same: measure the invariant, observe the failure mode, and choose a design response that keeps the system understandable under pressure. That is the language you will use in design review and in the Integrity Packet.
